title: Chef Kunal Kapur's Moong Dal Idli With Smoky Tomato Chutney Is the Breakfast Upgrade You Need
excerpt: Light, protein-packed, and naturally gluten-free, this golden idli recipe swaps traditional rice batter for soaked moong dal — with a charred tomato chutney that ties it all together.
body:
• Chef Kunal Kapur's moong dal idli replaces traditional rice-and-urad batter with soaked skinless moong dal, making it high in protein, naturally gluten-free, and lighter than the standard version.
  • The batter uses curd, ginger, green chilli, and a mustard-turmeric tempering, with grated carrots and coriander folded in before steaming for 10-12 minutes.
  • The smoky roasted tomato chutney is made by charring whole tomatoes and garlic in oil, then blending with Kashmiri chilli powder, black salt, onion, and lemon juice.
  • The full recipe was originally shared on Kapur's YouTube channel and requires no special equipment beyond an idli steamer.

Why Moong Dal Changes the Game

The standard idli relies on a fermented batter of rice and urad dal that needs overnight soaking and grinding. Chef Kunal Kapur's version takes a different path. By using skinless moong dal as the base, the recipe cuts preparation time and delivers a softer, golden idli that's packed with plant-based protein and is naturally gluten-free.

Kapur originally shared the recipe on his YouTube channel, and it has drawn attention for its simplicity — most of the ingredients are pantry staples in any Indian kitchen. The batter comes together in a blender after soaking the moong dal for two to three hours, and the idlis steam in just 10 to 12 minutes.

The Idli Batter

Soak one cup of skinless moong dal in water for two to three hours, then drain. Blend with a quarter cup of curd, chopped ginger, two green chillies, and about three-quarters of a cup of water until smooth. Transfer to a bowl and stir in a teaspoon of salt.

For the tempering, heat two tablespoons of oil and add half a teaspoon of asafoetida, a teaspoon of mustard seeds, a sprig of curry leaves, and half a teaspoon of turmeric. Pour the tempering into the batter and mix well.

Fold in a third of a cup of grated carrot and a handful of chopped coriander. Just before steaming, gently stir in a teaspoon of Eno or baking soda — the batter will turn light and airy. Grease idli moulds, fill them, and steam for 10 to 12 minutes until a toothpick comes out clean.

The Smoky Tomato Chutney

The chutney is what elevates the dish from simple to compelling. Heat three tablespoons of oil with asafoetida, mustard seeds, and cumin. Add six whole medium tomatoes, two green chillies, and five to six garlic cloves. Roast until the tomatoes are soft and charred and the garlic is fragrant.

Let it cool slightly, then blend or coarsely mash. Stir in a tablespoon of Kashmiri chilli powder, salt, three-quarters of a teaspoon of black salt, four tablespoons of chopped onion, fresh coriander, and four tablespoons of lemon juice. The result is tangy, smoky, and just spicy enough to complement the mild idlis.

Serving and Variations

Serve the idlis hot, straight from the steamer, with the chutney on the side. The moong dal base makes them lighter than traditional idlis, so they work well as a mid-morning snack or a light dinner alongside sambar or coconut chutney.

For additional texture, some cooks add finely chopped cashews or a tablespoon of semolina to the batter. The chutney keeps well in the refrigerator for two to three days, making it worth preparing in a larger batch.
